findings.suggestion: Extract `private URI acceptableTarget(String longUrl)` containing the three calls and have both create and createAnonymous call it. The design's reason for two public methods (different request/response types, different expiry) is unaffected — only the shared acceptance rule moves.
findings.summary: The three-call target-acceptance sequence (parseOrThrow / requireShortenable / requirePermittedTarget) is now written twice, in create and createAnonymous. AC12 requires the two paths to accept exactly the same targets, and the javadoc on createAnonymous asserts that in prose, but nothing in the code enforces it: a fourth check added to create in six months is silently absent from the anonymous path. This is duplication of the kind that drifts, and it is the security-relevant kind.

findings.suggestion: Add `private String shortUrl(String code)` and use it from both toResponse and the AnonymousLinkResponse construction; keep the two response builders separate since the DTOs genuinely differ.
findings.summary: createAnonymous builds its response inline while every other read path in the class goes through toResponse, and `baseUrl + "/" + link.getCode()` is now spelled in two places. The short-URL join is the sort of thing that acquires trailing-slash handling later in one copy only.

findings.suggestion: Throw IllegalStateException from the constructor when a non-null ownHost does not normalise (it is bean construction, so it fails the context rather than a request), or at minimum log.warn once naming the host and stating that the self-referential check is inactive.
findings.summary: `canonicalOwnHost = HostNormalizer.normalize(ownHost).orElse(null)` silently degrades: if app.base-url's host ever fails to canonicalise, the self-referential-target rule disappears at startup with no log line and no failure, and the only symptom is short links pointing at short links. Elsewhere this codebase is careful to log the moment a protection stops applying (see the fail-open warn in LinkService.requirePermittedTarget and JwtSessionService's ephemeral-key warning).

findings.suggestion: Have valueOf take the radix as a parameter (the caller can obtain it once) and return OptionalLong, or keep the long sentinel but name it (`private static final long NOT_AN_ADDRESS_PART = -1L`) so the two failure encodings are at least both self-describing.
findings.summary: Two different sentinel conventions live within twenty lines: radixOf returns NOT_A_NUMBER (0) and valueOf returns -1, so asDottedQuad has to test `part < 0` for one failure and callers test `== NOT_A_NUMBER` for the other. valueOf also recomputes radixOf for a part isAddressCandidate has already classified, so the classification exists twice.

findings.suggestion: Either rename to SignUpController to match SignInController and its service, or leave it and accept that customer-resource endpoints belong here. Worth one line either way; the current pairing is the only inconsistency.
findings.summary: CustomerController is named for the resource while its immediate sibling SignInController is named for the action, and it delegates to SignUpService. Nothing is wrong today — one endpoint, one collaborator — but the name promises the customer resource generally, so the next customer endpoint (GET /customers/{id}, password change) will land here by name rather than by cohesion.

not_examined: service/src/test/** — the test diff (~2,400 lines) is the test-adequacy reviewer's brief; I read it only where it clarified production intent
artifacts/openapi.yaml and the DTOs under api/ — frozen contract files owned by the API-contract lens
Correctness of the IPv4/IDN canonicalisation itself, and of the V3/V4 migrations against a real database — out of this lens's brief
Performance of the added query and hashing paths
summary: Clean change overall, and unusually well documented: the comments say why (NULL owner vs sentinel row in V4, hand-rolled IPv4 parsing, no Location header, the pre-apply duplicate check on V3) rather than what, and they match the house style of the surrounding code. Structure is right — business rules in SignUpService and LinkService, controllers only rate-limit and delegate; rate-limiting goes through the existing RateLimitGuard in the existing shape; log lines match SignInService's identity-free convention; no swallowed exceptions (the two catches translate a constraint violation and a dependency failure, both commented). The findings worth acting on are CLEAN-1 (the acceptance sequence duplicated between the owned and anonymous create paths, where AC12 requires them to agree and only prose enforces it) and CLEAN-3 (a security check that can silently switch itself off at startup). The remaining three are taste; the rest of the diff's minor points were consistent with the code around them and are not filed.
